title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals have used deepfake and voice-cloning technology to impersonate specific individuals and target vulnerable populations. A South Florida immigration attorney had his voice and identity cloned to deceive immigrants seeking legal services, and individuals lost thousands of dollars to fraudulent schemes. The technology allowed scammers to research personal relationships and fabricate legitimacy before making fraudulent requests.

This is a failure of AI systems to prevent misuse for impersonation and fraud. The deepfake technology was deployed without apparent safeguards to verify that the person using it had authorization to create synthetic media of real individuals. Catching this would have required technical controls on synthetic media generation, enforcement of identity verification before voice or image cloning, and rapid takedown processes for fraudulent accounts.

It is not established whether the companies providing the underlying AI tools knew their systems were being used for fraud, or what specific platforms hosted the fraudulent accounts.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to commit sophisticated scams across the country. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. High-profile cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target vulnerable immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency fraud scheme. The FBI received over 1 million internet crime complaints totaling more than $20 billion in reported losses overall.

The scams involve criminals using AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make fraudulent requests seem legitimate. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints resulting in $10.4 million in losses. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests directly through known phone numbers, avoid sending money based on phone calls alone, and report suspected scams to law enforcement or the FBI.
